{"id": "46:4/q30", "question": "What merit is reported for reciting al-Ahqaf?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "46:4/q30/p1", "position": "A report promises ten good deeds per grain of sand, ten sins erased, and ten ranks raised.", "reasons": "Jishumi transmits Ubayy b. {"id": "46:4/q31", "question": "What inward meanings are drawn from the verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "46:4/q31/p1", "position": "Ego and Satan cannot act in the self or spirit; God alone creates and turns hearts.", "reasons": "Bursevi maps earth to self and heavens to spirit."}, {"id": "46:4/q31/p2", "position": "Sincere worship seeks neither paradise as reward nor escape from Hell.", "reasons": "Bursevi says even reward- or fear-driven worship regards something besides God; he attributes agreement to outer and inner scholars."}]}
{"id": "46:4/q32", "question": "What unrelated reading or interpretive notices appear alongside the verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "46:4/q32/p1", "position": "Readers quiesce nine possessive yāʾs, including the one in Yusuf's يدعونني إليه.", "reasons": "Nashr records suggested difficulty from many successive letters and notes other explanations."}]}
{"id": "46:4/q33", "question": "How does al-Khuli's hermeneutic approach understand Quran interpretation?", "turns_on": "Whether interpretation receives a fixed meaning or is shaped by the interpreter's horizon.", "positions": [{"id": "46:4/q33/p1", "position": "Interpretation is active dialogue shaped by the reader's worldview, culture, expectations, and assumptions; tafsir should use literary and human sciences.", "reasons": "Rifai-Khuli says al-Khuli criticized sectarian instrumental tafsir, explored sociology and psychology, directed students toward the method, and formed al-Umana with Khalafallah, Bint al-Shati, and al-Alai. Later Arabic writers mainly used it in literary criticism; some experts feared clerical hostility to applying it to scripture."}, {"id": "46:4/q33/p2", "position": "Religious thought should be rebuilt first by clergy familiar with the tradition.", "reasons": "Rifai-Khuli says their knowledge and concern equip them for the task and compares Tahtawi's clerical mediation of Western ideas."}]}
{"id": "46:4/q34", "question": "What intellectual history does the al-Khuli note give for modern hermeneutics?", "turns_on": "What influence on al-Khuli can be documented versus inferred.", "positions": [{"id": "46:4/q34/p1", "position": "German modern hermeneutics runs from Schleiermacher through Dilthey and Heidegger to Gadamer; al-Khuli may have encountered it during his stay in Germany.", "reasons": "Rifai-Khuli recounts al-Khuli's imam posts in Rome and Berlin, his return in 1927, German philosophy's influence, and Shabestari's later Hamburg path. He notes al-Khuli did not document his encounter; Ahmad Khalil identified Schleiermacher parallels, strengthening the author's inference. Heidegger and Gadamer treat understanding as ontological."}]}
{"id": "46:4/q35", "question": "How does مَّا refer to multiple worshipped objects?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "46:4/q35/p1", "position": "The relative mā has a collective, plural sense.", "reasons": "Majaz explicitly analyzes mā as collective."}]}
{"id": "46:4/q36", "question": "Do Jesus's extraordinary acts amount to independent divine creation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "46:4/q36/p1", "position": "No; Jesus revived the dead and made a bird only through God's power and permission.", "reasons": "Bursevi says those miracles do not remove Jesus's own incapacity."}]}
{"id": "46:4/q37", "question": "What ancient witness is sought for the idols' right to worship?", "turns_on": "Whether the witness is specified as prophetic instruction or inherited learning in general.", "positions": [{"id": "46:4/q37/p1", "position": "A transmitted report from earlier prophets commanding worship of other than God, or ancient learning supporting their right to worship.", "reasons": "Wahidi-Wajiz specifies a prophetic command; Baydawi accepts ancient learning for either entitlement or command."}, {"id": "46:4/q37/p2", "position": "Inherited knowledge.", "reasons": "Mawardi transmits Ikrima's gloss without specifying its content."}]}
{"id": "46:4/q38", "question": "What line-drawing identification was transmitted for أَثَٰرَةٍ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "46:4/q38/p1", "position": "Ibn Abbas identified it with lines drawn in earth for Arab divination, and Tabari knew a prophetic interpretation as line-drawing.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says Arabs used the marks for omens; Tabari promises to cite the report later."}]}
{"id": "50:3/q01", "question": "What answer to the opening oath is understood here?", "turns_on": "Whether the oath's implied answer states resurrection alone or embraces the ensuing message about prophethood as well.", "positions": [{"id": "50:3/q01/p1", "position": "They will certainly be raised after death.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ says the oath supplies the assertion the deniers contest; Ibn Qutayba cites omission of an oath's answer when later words reveal it, comparing 79:1 and 79:6. Al-Qushayrī gives it as a proposed answer."}, {"id": "50:3/q01/p2", "position": "The ensuing message establishes both prophethood and resurrection.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr prefers the answer implicit in what follows and compares the Qur'anic oath in 38:1–2."}]}
{"id": "50:3/q02", "question": "What do the unbelievers find astonishing before this objection, and how does 50:3 follow it?", "turns_on": "Whether the earlier 'this is strange' points chiefly to the arriving warner or also to his warning of resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "50:3/q02/p1", "position": "They marvel at a human warner; their resurrection objection then dismisses his warning.", "reasons": "Rāzī says Ṣād's wonder follows the demand to make the gods one, whereas Qāf's follows the warner's arrival; taking both expressions as wonder at resurrection would repeat the point. He distinguishes the nearby 'this' (the present warner) from distant 'that' (future return), cites 11:73 and 34:43, and notes their accusations against the messenger. Elmalılı makes the connective explanatory and 'this' the warning. Iṣlāḥī says resistance to accepting a messenger from their own community drives the objection. Al-Biqāʿī says astonishment rather than rejection of the Qur'an's glory or the Prophet's truth is foregrounded. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the earlier 'this' points to the Prophet's call to believe in resurrection, which 50:3 spells out."}, {"id": "50:3/q02/p2", "position": "Their astonishment also concerns the resurrection announced by the warner.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, as reported by Rāzī, takes 'this is strange' as a second expression of wonder at resurrection and its warning. Al-Ṭabrisī mentions both a messenger from their people and resurrection. Elmalılı makes the connective coordinate the two wonders; Ṭabāṭabāʾī permits either the human warner or true Resurrection after the turn from the omitted oath answer."}]}

Ibn Jinnī understands the return as implausible to them, not temporally distant."}, {"id": "50:3/q04/p3", "position": "The one-hamza form can remain interrogative if the interrogative hamza is omitted.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, and al-Ālūsī report this possibility. {"id": "50:3/q05", "question": "What completes and governs the construction beginning with أَءِذَا?", "turns_on": "The reading of idhā and whether the final clause belongs to the deniers or to God's answer determine its omitted completion and governor.", "positions": [{"id": "50:3/q05/p1", "position": "An implied verb or predicate asks whether they will be raised or returned when dead and dust.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj says idhā needs a governing verb. Al-Akhfash treats the question as their response to an implied 'you will return'; al-Thalabī and al-Baghawī say context supplies resurrection. Al-Ṭabrisī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, al-Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī supply 'will we be raised/returned?' Al-Qurṭubī also describes an omitted repetition of their objection and says the warner's warning and the Qur'an's unity suffice without an immediately preceding mention of resurrection. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports Ibn Jinnī's 'when we die, are we then returned?' Al-Wāḥidī calls it an interrogative denial with omitted answer."}, {"id": "50:3/q05/p2", "position": "On the declarative reading, the answer after idhā is omitted: they will return.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī supply the omitted response. Ibn Jinnī and al-Zamakhsharī also construe the one-hamza form as a statement of return after death and dust."}, {"id": "50:3/q05/p3", "position": "On the declarative reading, 'that is a distant return' itself answers idhā.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says it is the predicate. Al-Samīn reports deletion of the expected fāʾ; al-Ālūsī attributes permission for it to the author of al-Lawāmiḥ. Both say the majority of grammarians allow such deletion only in poetry."}, {"id": "50:3/q05/p4", "position": "If the final words are God's reply, idhā is governed by resurrection implied in the warner's warning.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī says the implied resurrection matter governs the time adverb. Al-Samīn repeats this; al-Ālūsī says the deniers' answer itself proves that they were warned of resurrection, meeting the objection that idhā has no governor."}]}
{"id": "50:3/q06", "question": "What is the force of their question about death and dust?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "50:3/q06/p1", "position": "It is astonished denial of bodily resurrection, not a request for information.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Farrāʾ, Ibn Qutayba, al-Qushayrī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Nasafī, al-Rāzī, Bursevī, al-Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, Asad, and Study Quran describe rejection or incredulity. Rāzī says the warner's threat of lasting punishment entails resurrection. Ibn Jarīr, reported by Ibn al-Jawzī, links their amazement at the warning to their denial of Muhammad and says they would learn the outcome on being raised. Ibn Jurayj reports that they asked who could restore them. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the omitted question makes the claim seem barely worth uttering; he compares 32:10. Study Quran compares 17:49, 36:78, 37:16–17, 37:53, 56:47, and 79:11."}]}
{"id": "50:3/q07", "question": "How is مِتْنَا pronounced?", "turns_on": "The alternative stem patterns of māta, and the resulting vowel on the mīm.", "positions": [{"id": "50:3/q07/p1", "position": "Mitnā has kasra on the mīm.", "reasons": "The Qirāʾāt note calls it the alternative a-stem form of the verb. Al-Nasafī reports a vowel form from Nāfiʿ, ʿAlī, Ḥamza, and Ḥafṣ without spelling that form in the extracted note."}, {"id": "50:3/q07/p2", "position": "Mutnā has ḍamma on the mīm.", "reasons": "The Qirāʾāt note derives it from the u-stem māta/yamūtu pattern and calls it standard in Ḥijāz."}]}
{"id": "50:3/q08", "question": "What does becoming تُرَابًۭا describe?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "50:3/q08/p1", "position": "Their bodies decay into dust or indistinguishable earthly remains.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī glosses dust as decayed remains. Ibn ʿĀshūr says this bodily decay is the timing on which they base their wonder; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says it appears to erase their identity without trace."}]}
{"id": "50:3/q09", "question": "What does ذَٰلِكَ رَجْعٌ mean, and whose judgment does the clause give?", "turns_on": "Whether rajʿ denotes the promised return or a returned reply, and whether the sentence is the deniers' speech or God's assessment.", "positions": [{"id": "50:3/q09/p1", "position": "The deniers call the resurrection or return to life a distant return.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī, al-Ālūsī, and al-Rāzī take 'that' as the warned-of resurrection. Al-Rāzī distinguishes transitive rajʿ from intransitive rujuʿ and rujʿā, while allowing intransitive rajʿ; he cites 96:8 and 79:10 for return or raising. Al-Bayḍāwī also allows 'the returned thing'."}, {"id": "50:3/q09/p2", "position": "God calls their reply denying resurrection itself outlandish or distant.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī proposes rajʿ as a returned answer; al-Nasafī allows response and says a pause after 'dust' is good. Abū Ḥayyān calls the interpretation astonishing and unintelligible to Arabs; al-Samīn reports the Shaykh's criticism, and al-Ālūsī deems rajʿ as 'reply' remote."}]}
{"id": "50:3/q10", "question": "What does بَعِيدٌ mean in their verdict?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "50:3/q10/p1", "position": "They consider resurrection far beyond experience or imagination, and therefore impossible.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, cited by al-Naḥḥās, says baʿīd can mean it will not happen, a recognized Arabic usage; al-Farrāʾ compares being far from the truth in an answer. Ibn Qutayba, al-Zajjāj, al-Qushayrī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Zamakhsharī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Ālūsī, Elmalılı, Ibn ʿĀshūr, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī variously stress implausibility, custom, thought, reason, or impossibility. {"id": "50:3/q12", "question": "What underlies the deniers' resistance to resurrection?", "turns_on": "Whether the notes explain the objection by imagined bodily impossibility or by resistance to the warner.", "positions": [{"id": "50:3/q12/p1", "position": "They find restoration after bodily decay inconceivable.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr describes the loss of bodily form and severed limbs; al-Biqāʿī and Bursevī picture the soul separated and the body indistinguishable from earth. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says they imagine no trace of identity remains; Asad summarizes the question as how return after dust is possible."}, {"id": "50:3/q12/p2", "position": "Pride and reluctance to accept a messenger from their own people drive the objection.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says accusations of poetry and soothsaying pretextually dismiss the Qur'an despite its grandeur and divine origin; arrogance prevents recognizing revelation and its arguments. {"id": "50:11/q01", "question": "What is the provision mentioned here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "50:11/q01/p1", "position": "The rain-grown gardens, grain, palm fruit, and other plants provide sustenance for God's servants.", "reasons": "Muqatil says all the growth is provision. Mawardi includes blessed rain, plants, harvested grain, and clustered palm fruit; Study Quran likewise includes water. Abu Hayyan distinguishes recurring produce, one- or two-year crops, and mixed kinds, noting crops are mostly food and fruits mostly treats. Ibn Kathir extends the beneficiaries to all creatures. Tabatabai defines sustenance as what maintains life. Qurtubi defines provision as what is made ready for use. Tabrisi says all provision comes from God's direct action or causation, though ordinary speech may attribute provision to people."}]}
{"id": "50:11/q02", "question": "How is rizqan construed grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the accusative states the purpose of growth, names the provision constituted by growth or an implied providing verb, or describes a circumstance.", "positions": [{"id": "50:11/q02/p1", "position": "It is an accusative of purpose: the plants were grown to provide sustenance.", "reasons": "Abu Ishaq, reported by Zajjaj, Nahhas, and Wahidi, gives this as an alternative. Kashshaf, Razi, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Nasafi, and Samin also give it. Alusi chooses it and says it modifies the preceding 'We caused to grow'; Ibn Ashur calls it an infinitive expressing God's purpose to sustain people, and Tabatabai applies it to gardens, grain, and palms."}, {"id": "50:11/q02/p2", "position": "It is a cognate or substitute verbal noun: growing these plants itself constitutes provision.", "reasons": "Abu Ishaq supplies an implied 'We provided them provision,' according to Zajjaj and Wahidi; Nahhas calls it a verbal noun. Kashshaf says growing entails providing. Razi, Baydawi, Nasafi, and Samin tie the noun to 'We caused to grow,' though it is not formed from that verb; Alusi compares 'I sat a sitting' (qaʿadtu julūsan). Ibn Atiyya simply calls it an accusative verbal noun. Qurtubi allows either an implied 'We provided' or a complement of the planting."}, {"id": "50:11/q02/p3", "position": "It is a circumstantial accusative, meaning 'provided for' or 'possessing provision.'", "reasons": "Samin reports both formulations; Alusi reports the first as an alternative."}]}
{"id": "50:11/q03", "question": "How does li-l-ʿibād attach to the construction?", "turns_on": "The syntactic role of the prepositional phrase in relation to rizqan.", "positions": [{"id": "50:11/q03/p1", "position": "It qualifies rizqan as an adjective.", "reasons": "Samin lists this attachment."}, {"id": "50:11/q03/p2", "position": "It attaches to the verbal noun rizqan.", "reasons": "Samin lists this attachment."}, {"id": "50:11/q03/p3", "position": "It is the verbal noun's object, with an additional lām.", "reasons": "Samin lists this analysis."}]}

{"id": "50:11/q05", "question": "Why is provision mentioned at this point?", "turns_on": "The notes give distinct purposes for naming provision: benefit, universal reach, priority of reflection, rebuke of denial, provision after resurrection, or reassurance.", "positions": [{"id": "50:11/q05/p1", "position": "It names the benefit and favor of the plants God created.", "reasons": "Razi says fruit's benefit is obvious, while the sky's provision is less obvious though decreed by God and accompanied by other benefits. {"id": "50:11/q07", "question": "How is 'We revived' connected to what precedes?", "turns_on": "Whether the coordination reaches back to the previous explicit verb or to the verbal sense of rizqan.", "positions": [{"id": "50:11/q07/p1", "position": "It is coordinated with 'We caused to grow by it' in the previous verse.", "reasons": "Razi identifies the preceding verbal clause in 50:9 as its syntactic partner."}, {"id": "50:11/q07/p2", "position": "It is coordinated with the derived noun rizqan, whose verbal sense is 'We provided.'", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur construes the sense as 'God provided people and revived land.'"}]}

{"id": "50:11/q15", "question": "How does the revival of land explain resurrection?", "turns_on": "The evidence can be the observed parallel of revived land, God's greater first creation, or the knowledge and power displayed in providence; the notes often combine them.", "positions": [{"id": "50:11/q15/p1", "position": "As rain visibly brings dead land and plants to life, God can bring dead people out of graves.", "reasons": "Muqatil compares emergence through water with plants; Wahidi cites 7:57. Ibn Kathir says the witnessed sign is clearer to deniers, citing 40:57, 46:33, and 41:39; Bursevi reports Kashifi's reflection on a buried seed. Study Quran cites 30:19, 16:65, 25:48–49, 30:50, 35:9, 36:33, 43:11, and 45:5."}, {"id": "50:11/q15/p2", "position": "The Creator of these things can create people again; restoring existing bodies is easier than creating from nothing.", "reasons": "Zajjaj and Nahhas state the inference from creation. Ibn Ashur says these beings' creation from nothing proves possible the restoration of already existing, weaker beings. Kuran Yolu adds that God knows what remains or decays in each body and can restore its like and return its soul; Islahi invokes 17:99 and 79:27–33."}, {"id": "50:11/q15/p3", "position": "The detailed provision displays God's knowledge, planning, and power, so dispersed human particles remain within His ability to restore.", "reasons": "Tabatabai calls this the earlier proof, distinct from the subsequent proof by analogy. {"id": "50:11/q16", "question": "What reports describe rain in relation to people and resurrection?", "turns_on": "The reported details differ: an unspecified seminal rain, a forty-night rain with bodily regrowth, or a general rain-and-plant comparison.", "positions": [{"id": "50:11/q16/p1", "position": "Rain falls like seminal fluid, and flesh and bones grow on the dead.", "reasons": "Wahidi reports this from Ibn Abbas; no number of nights is specified."}, {"id": "50:11/q16/p2", "position": "God sends rain for forty nights; it enters the earth like male seed, grows flesh, veins, and bones, then God revives and brings people out.", "reasons": "Bursevi gives this as an unattributed report."}, {"id": "50:11/q16/p3", "position": "People emerge from graves through rain as plants emerge through rain.", "reasons": "Wahidi transmits Muqatil's comparison; Muqatil's own note likewise describes emergence through water."}]}

{"id": "50:11/q20", "question": "How does the word khurūj answer the denial in 50:3?", "turns_on": "Whether rajʿ in 50:3 is intransitive return or implies God's act of extraction, whose effect is emergence.", "positions": [{"id": "50:11/q20/p1", "position": "Its wording supports taking the deniers' rajʿ as intransitive 'return.'", "reasons": "Razi prefers this: if they had denied God's extracting people, the reply would suitably have used ikhrāj, but it uses khurūj."}, {"id": "50:11/q20/p2", "position": "Khurūj names the effect of extraction; denying extraction entails denying emergence, so the verse emphatically affirms that effect.", "reasons": "Razi gives this alternative if 50:3 is understood as denial of extraction and its result."}]}
{"id": "50:11/q21", "question": "How does this verse fit the passage's argument?", "turns_on": "The notes explain the sequence as a move from observable signs to conclusion, or account more specifically for the order of provision and revival and the final clause's discourse role.", "positions": [{"id": "50:11/q21/p1", "position": "The passage moves from resurrection-denial to visible signs in heaven, earth, rain, and revived land, then concludes that emergence is likewise possible.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Zubayr, reported by Burhan, links the move from 50:1 to 50:6 and 50:9 with signs deniers cannot dispute; Burhan says their challenge is left unanswered until the concluding phrase. Ibn Ashur says the shift from heaven and earth to repeated life-and-death cycles prepares the proof. Tabatabai says the passage recalls God's knowledge and power in adorned heaven, spread and planted earth, and providential rain. Islahi calls land's revival the sura's central theme; Kuran Yolu says the broader passage answers denial through creation, knowledge, power, and blessings."}, {"id": "50:11/q21/p2", "position": "The provision evidence precedes the land-revival proof because heaven and earth already established resurrection; crops and fruit are mentioned before the land's greenery as the greater blessing.", "reasons": "Razi reports the first ordering explanation, then an alternative: water first makes land green and flowery, a more widespread adornment, but crops and fruit appear first in the wording for their greater benefit."}, {"id": "50:11/q21/p3", "position": "The final clause resumes and summarizes the preceding proof of resurrection, possibly as a parenthetical close.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur prefers resumption, allowing a parenthesis for grammarians who recognize it."}]}
{"id": "50:11/q22", "question": "What further teaching do these signs carry?", "turns_on": "The notes draw both recognition of divine attributes and the duty of accountability from the same signs.", "positions": [{"id": "50:11/q22/p1", "position": "They reveal God's oneness, power, wisdom, and providence and call for reflection and gratitude.", "reasons": "Muqatil says rain and growth disclose oneness and resurrection power. {"id": "50:11/q23", "question": "What further symbolic revival is read in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the further revived subject is a community through Islam's victory or spiritually dead hearts.", "positions": [{"id": "50:11/q23/p1", "position": "It alludes to Islam's emergence and victory through divine favor, giving new life to a dead community.", "reasons": "Elmalılı offers this additional allusion."}, {"id": "50:11/q23/p2", "position": "The earth's revival can symbolize God's revival of spiritually dead hearts.", "reasons": "Study Quran offers this as an additional symbolic sense."}]}
{"id": "51:2/q01", "question": "What does al-ḥāmilāt mean as a word?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "51:2/q01/p1", "position": "Those that carry a burden.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu gives the literal sense as carriers of a load or weight."}, {"id": "51:2/q01/p2", "position": "The word can describe pregnant females.", "reasons": "Jishumi distinguishes ḥaml, a womb or tree load, from ḥiml, a load on the back, and cites a poem using ḥāmilah of a pregnant woman. {"id": "51:2/q02", "question": "Who or what are the burden bearers?", "turns_on": "Whether the participle denotes the rain-laden cloud, its moving wind, a loaded ship, a pregnant creature, or a wider set of causes; the wind and cloud sequence and the scope of the plural are cited.", "positions": [{"id": "51:2/q02/p1", "position": "Rain-bearing clouds.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Ali, Ibn Abbas and later commentators identify clouds. Biqai describes wind dispersing and gathering vapor into clouds bearing water, lightning, and other unseen contents. {"id": "51:2/q03", "question": "What does wiqr mean?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish kasra wiqr for a burden from fatḥa waqr for ear heaviness.", "positions": [{"id": "51:2/q03/p1", "position": "A heavy carried load, especially on the back or in the belly.", "reasons": "Nahhas says any load on the back; Mawardi, Tabrisi, Qurtubi and Tabatabai include the womb or belly. {"id": "51:2/q04", "question": "How is wiqran read and explained in the variant reading?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "51:2/q04/p1", "position": "It is read waqran with fatḥa on the wāw.", "reasons": "Kashshaf and Baydawi say the verbal noun names the carried thing, in place of ḥamlan; Samin reports both this object-naming explanation and the possibility of a verbal noun governed by the preceding sense of carrying, since ḥaml and waqr overlap though ḥaml is broader."}]}
{"id": "51:2/q05", "question": "What grammatical role does wiqran have?", "turns_on": "Whether the word names the thing carried as an object or, with fatḥa, retains its verbal-noun force.", "positions": [{"id": "51:2/q05/p1", "position": "It is the object of al-ḥāmilāt.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Nasafi, Samin and Bursevi explicitly parse it as the carried object; Nasafi and Bursevi combine this with the cloud reading."}, {"id": "51:2/q05/p2", "position": "Under the fatḥa reading, it can remain a verbal noun governed by the preceding verbal meaning.", "reasons": "Samin says ḥaml and waqr overlap in sense, though ḥaml is broader."}]}

{"id": "51:2/q07", "question": "What does the fāʾ sequence imply about the four oath descriptions?", "turns_on": "Whether fāʾ orders different classes of creatures or successive properties and actions of a single subject; Islahi invokes an Arabic rule, while the reported Ali interpretation supplies distinct referents.", "positions": [{"id": "51:2/q07/p1", "position": "It orders distinct referents and the effects or signs linking them.", "reasons": "Kashshaf orders winds, the clouds they drive, ships moved by wind, and angels apportioning provision through rain and trade. {"id": "51:2/q08", "question": "What is the oath's answer and what does it affirm?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "51:2/q08/p1", "position": "What people are promised is true, and judgment or recompense will occur.", "reasons": "Zajjaj cites 51:5; Qushayri says the promised thing is true; Kuranyolu cites 51:5–6 for the certain Day of Judgment. {"id": "51:2/q09", "question": "Why are these things sworn by, and what do they show?", "turns_on": "The notes variously stress signs of divine power, evidence for resurrection, reflection and affirmation, and Farahi's theory of an oath's semantic purpose.", "positions": [{"id": "51:2/q09/p1", "position": "They display God's making, power, blessings, and wise governance, inviting reflection.", "reasons": "Jishumi says winds and clouds show power and blessings; Baghawi says created things demonstrate God's making and power. Tabrisi cites their human benefits and signs of oneness and artistry. Biqai says measured winds, suspended clouds, ship movement, and angelic distribution show a wise Creator; excess, cessation, or stillness can destroy. Kuranyolu links the oaths to earthly and heavenly provision and the surah's 51:22, citing 51:7, 20, 23, 47, 48."}, {"id": "51:2/q09/p2", "position": "The displayed power and extraordinary order establish God's ability to resurrect.", "reasons": "Biqai reports Baydawi's inference from extraordinary phenomena; Kuranyolu repeats it as the inference from striking order and balance."}, {"id": "51:2/q09/p3", "position": "The oath strengthens belief and prompts thought, while a human oath calls God as witness.", "reasons": "Biqai reports Razi contrasting divine oaths by created wonders with human oaths by God, who knows claims in public and secret.
